title: Kutuzov Gives Up Moscow
text:
On 7 September 1812 the Russian army under Mikhail Kutuzov fought Napoleon's Grande Armee at Borodino, west of Moscow. It was one of the bloodiest days of the century, and both armies were badly mauled. Napoleon held the field, and the road to Moscow lay open.

A week later Kutuzov held a council of war in a peasant's hut at the village of Fili. Several generals wanted to fight again in front of the city. Kutuzov decided otherwise: as long as the army existed, Russia could still win the war; if the army was destroyed defending Moscow, both would be lost. He ordered the retreat through the city, and most of the inhabitants left with it.

Napoleon entered Moscow on 14 September and found it nearly empty. Fires broke out that night and burned much of the city, widely believed to have been set on Russian orders. Napoleon waited for Tsar Alexander to ask for peace. No answer came. Meanwhile Kutuzov moved his army south to Tarutino, where it rested, received reinforcements and covered the rich southern provinces.

In mid October, with winter approaching and supplies failing, Napoleon left Moscow. Blocked from the southern route, he retreated along the devastated road he had come by, harried by Kutuzov's army and Cossacks. Only a small fraction of the Grande Armee left Russia.
lesson: Do not confuse the symbol with the thing that actually decides the outcome. Giving up what looks most important can preserve what really is.
people: Mikhail Kutuzov, Napoleon Bonaparte, Alexander I
source: Dominic Lieven, Russia Against Napoleon (2009); Carl von Clausewitz, The Campaign of 1812 in Russia
